title: Ars Pythonica
text:
Introduction
Ars Pythonica offers an introduction to programming in Python aimed at classical philologists who work with Greek and Latin texts and seek to incorporate digital humanities and distant reading methods into their research. No prior programming experience is required.
By the end, you should be able to read and write code and understand what it does, find and fix errors, be familiar with the fundamentals of Python syntax, apply basic pre-processing, data extraction, and data normalization methods, perform exploratory data analysis, and take first steps in using distant reading tools on your own textual corpora.

title: Ars Pythonica
text:
How the course works
This book is a supplement to twelve weekly sessions of 90 minutes, plus an optional final hackathon-style session, during which we will aim to create, clean up, and structure your research corpora.
The course is structured as a flipped classroom: you learn the concepts at home via interactive courses, while in the session we do a quick recap, address challenges and issues, and then apply the newly acquired skills together to Greek and Latin texts.

At home:

in Part I, assignments from futurecoder and Exercism, up to the checkpoint given in the schedule;
in Part II, TBA.

In the session: a quick concept check, troubleshooting, hands-on workshop (e.g. installation, IDE setup, Jupyter notebooks, CLI, data extraction, corpus cleanup etc.), debugging, and results review.

Every session is still useful if you didn’t manage the home assignments, but it is nevertheless recommended to complete the basic exercises, since coding is a practical skill.

title: Ars Pythonica
text:
Using AI






TipGeneral practice



You can use AI to explain, not to code.


The aim of this course is not to produce impeccable coding solutions to problems, rather to allow participants to break code and experience as many errors as possible through practice and active debugging.
Therefore, the use of AI is allowed on an honor system. To make it practical, feel free to use this tutor prompt or set it as custom instructions if you decide to use AI:
I'm learning Python. Explain concepts and error messages, and ask me guiding questions. Don't give me the solution right away, don't write or fix code for me.

title: Setup
text:
1. Python
Before session 2, install two things: Python and the VS Code editor. Then run a two-line script to check that everything works.
We use Python 3.14 from python.org. It comes with IDLE, the simple editor we open in session 2.

title: Setup
text:
WindowsmacOS



Download the Python install manager from python.org/downloads/windows and install it.
Open Terminal / PowerShell or Command Prompt from the Start menu and type:
py install 3.14
If it asks whether to add a folder to PATH or change other settings, accept.
Check the installation:
py --version
It should print Python 3.14. followed by a number.

IDLE is now in the Start menu under Python 3.14 → IDLE (Python 3.14).
If the install manager gives you trouble, the same page still offers the classic Windows installer (64-bit) for Python 3.14. On its first screen, tick Add python.exe to PATH before clicking Install Now.



Download the macOS installer for the latest Python 3.14 from python.org/downloads/macos and run it, accepting the defaults.
At the end, a Finder window opens the folder Applications → Python 3.14. Double-click Install Certificates.command there; it lets Python download files from the internet.
Open Terminal (in Applications → Utilities) and check the installation:
python3 --version
It should print Python 3.14. followed by a number.

IDLE is in Applications → Python 3.14 → IDLE.









NoteAlready using conda?



If you already work with Anaconda, Miniconda or Miniforge, you can keep it: create an environment with conda create -n ars-pythonica python=3.14 and select it in VS Code (see section 3). The instructions in this book assume the python.org installation, so details may differ for you.

title: Setup
text:
2. VS Code
VS Code is the editor we use from session 2 on. It needs the Python extension to run Python code.

WindowsmacOS



Download the Windows User Installer from code.visualstudio.com/download and run it. Keep Add to PATH ticked.
Open VS Code, press Ctrl+Shift+X (Extensions), search for Python, and install the extension by Microsoft.
Search for Jupyter and install the extension by Microsoft, so that VS Code can open Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files).




Download the Mac version from code.visualstudio.com/download, open the download, and move Visual Studio Code into Applications.
Open VS Code, press Cmd+Shift+X (Extensions), search for Python, and install the extension by Microsoft.
Search for Jupyter and install the extension by Microsoft, so that VS Code can open Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files).










NoteDon’t forget about ipykernel



When you create or open an .ipynb notebook for the first time and run any cell, VS Code may prompt you to install ipykernel - this package is necessary to execute Jupyter notebook code. Accept and install.

title: 1  What is Python?
text:
1.1 Why code?
What makes Python so appealing, useful, and flexible for scholarly research and textual analysis?
Is it the best programming language?
Better yet, does it even make sense to study programming in the age of AI?
We use programming to solve computational problems or perform specific tasks (oftentimes repetitive or routine) by providing a computer with step-by-step instructions.
Communication between humans and computers is defined by I/O that stands for “input/output” and generally covers the broad spectrum of interfaces, peripherals and agents involved in this process, such as human operators, information processing systems, and AI agents.

title: 1  What is Python?
text:
NoteI/O in different programming languages





This article gives a brief comparison of how different programming languages like C, JS, or Python handle input/output. You may notice that Python doesn’t require a standalone library for that – another testament to its popularity!

title: 1  What is Python?
text:
1.2 Why code manually?
Suffice it to say, LLMs are here to stay. The performance of frontier models improves constantly, and they excel at automating routine tasks, drafting boilerplates, and a vast range of generation tasks, such as summarisation, Q&A, or RAG.
The benchmarks below (courtesy of Christopher Pollin, who talked about AI workflows at MLDSE 2026 in Graz) demonstrate three trends in the current snapshot of frontier LLM models.
Growing capabilities
Over the years, frontier LLMs have learnt to handle tasks with more advanced computational complexity, as demonstrated on this chart prepared by the METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) nonprofit community, who monitor frontier models performance (Figure 1.1).
There is a steadily growing trend in task-completion time horizon, and the growth is even steeper on a linear scale (Figure 1.2).

Log scaleLinear scale








Figure 1.1: Task-completion time horizons of frontier AI models: the length of task (measured by how long it takes a human expert) that a model is predicted to complete with 50% success, represented on a logarithmic scale. Based on METR’s Time Horizon 1.1 suite of software engineering, machine learning and cybersecurity tasks. Screenshot of the interactive chart at metr.org/time-horizons, data as of 8 May 2026.











Figure 1.2: Task-completion time horizons of frontier AI models: the length of task (measured by how long it takes a human expert) that a model is predicted to complete with 50% success, represented on a linear scale. Based on METR’s Time Horizon 1.1 suite of software engineering, machine learning and cybersecurity tasks. Screenshot of the interactive chart at metr.org/time-horizons, data as of 8 May 2026.






Jagged capabilities
Performance, however, is uneven. The same models that can work through software tasks lasting many hours still stumble on problems most people solve without effort. These results are often described as jagged: excellent at some tasks, surprisingly weak at closely related ones, with no reliable way to tell in advance which is which.
On SimpleBench (Figure 1.3), a set of trick questions on everyday spatial, temporal and social reasoning, only the three best models have overtaken the average human baseline of 83.7%, and none comes close to the best human score of 95.4%.
The gap is wider still on ARC-AGI-3 (Figure 1.4), whose game-like environments are designed to be easy for humans to pick up: most systems score below 10%, and only a few approach human level, with a dedicated harness and at a cost of thousands of dollars. For us, this unevenness is the practical point: an AI assistant may solve one coding problem flawlessly and fail at the next without warning, so we need to be able to read, test and fix its code ourselves.






NoteJagged technology frontier



The term “jagged” was first introduced in (Dell’Acqua et al. 2023), who define the concept of a “jagged technology frontier” to describe the uneven impact of GPT-4 models.



Dell’Acqua, Fabrizio, Edward McFowland Iii, Ethan R. Mollick, et al. 2023. “Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of Artificial Intelligence on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality.” Pre-published. https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.4573321.

Everyday reasoningUnfamiliar tasks (AGI)








Figure 1.3: Top ten language models on SimpleBench, a multiple-choice benchmark of over 200 questions on spatio-temporal reasoning, social intelligence and trick questions that people with ordinary high-school knowledge can answer. Scores are averaged over five runs (AVG@5). Screenshot of the leaderboard at simple-bench.com, as of 2 October 2026.











Figure 1.4: Scores of AI systems on ARC-AGI-3, an interactive reasoning benchmark of game-like environments that agents must learn from experience; a score of 100% means beating every game as efficiently as humans. Scores are plotted against cost per task, represented on a logarithmic scale; dashed lines connect the same model at different reasoning levels. Screenshot of the leaderboard at arcprize.org/leaderboard, as of 3 October 2026.






Asymmetric amplification
In his blogpost (Pollin 2026), Christopher Pollin argues that frontier models do not so much automate research as amplify computer-based research work, and that they do so unevenly:

Pollin, Christopher. 2026. “Asymmetric Amplification. Why AI Does Not Automate Research – But Disruptively Amplifies Computer-Based Research Work.” Digital Humanities Craft; Digital Humanities Craft, February 9. https://dhcraft.org/excellence/blog/Asymmetric-Amplification/.

“Those who can judge quality, who understand their data and their domain, and who have access to frontier models and the infrastructure behind them, gain disproportionate leverage. Those who cannot are left behind.”

A model multiplies the skills its user already brings: where there are none, there is little to multiply. And since a model produces plausible text without checking it, someone still has to verify the result, or, as Pollin puts it, “without Computer Literacy, the first error message is a dead end.” He describes three layers of competence that build on each other: computer literacy, computational thinking, and informed vibe coding, that is, working critically with a model on the basis of the first two.
We will focus on the first two layers, so that the third becomes useful, controlled, and productive.

title: 1  What is Python?
1  What is Python?
text:
1.4 History
Python began as a holiday project. In December 1989, Guido van Rossum, a programmer at the Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica (CWI) in Amsterdam, was looking for something to keep him busy over Christmas. He had helped build ABC, a teaching language developed at CWI, and Python took over several of its ideas, among them indentation as grammar and very high-level data types. The first public version, 0.9.0, followed in February 1991.
The name has nothing to do with reptiles. Van Rossum was reading the published scripts of Monty Python’s Flying Circus and wanted a name that was “short, unique, and slightly mysterious”. The official tutorial still encourages references to the show, which is why example variables in Python documentation are so often called spam and eggs.

By the way, the language is named after the BBC show “Monty Python’s Flying Circus” and has nothing to do with reptiles. Making references to Monty Python skits in documentation is not only allowed, it is encouraged!

In December 2008, Python 3.0 broke compatibility with earlier versions to fix old design flaws, and one fix was that all text became Unicode. In Python 2, a Greek word was by default a sequence of bytes: len('Μῆνιν') gave 11 instead of 5. The switch took more than a decade, and Python 2 reached its end of life on 1 January 2020.
Van Rossum stepped down as the language’s “Benevolent Dictator For Life” in 2018. Since then, an elected Steering Council has guided Python’s development, with a new version every October. This course uses Python 3.14.
